items.t: Promontory is the Sardis hillside east of Vedder Road, reached by Promontory Road, and that hillside position east of the Vedder corridor is what separates it from the flat Sardis streets.

The BC Transit Route 54 map names the Promontory timing points a buyer will use to place the area: Vedder Road at Promontory Road at the bottom of the hill, and Teskey Way at Promontory Road on the hillside.
Vedder Road is the primary transportation spine of the Sardis neighbourhood, providing the main north-south connection within and out of Sardis, and Promontory Road branches east from it.

The City's Official Community Plan (OCP) lists the Eastern Hillsides Neighbourhood Plan as Schedule B4 and the Sardis Neighbourhood Plan as Schedule B5 as separate schedules, so a Promontory lot's plan cover must be read lot by lot rather than assumed.
No City, School District No. 33 (SD33) or developer source publishes a Promontory-wide build decade, lot-size or style profile, so none is claimed here.

The housing-form fact the City does state for the hillside is permit-based, not stock-based: the hillside development permit area applies to new construction and earthworks on slopes of 20% or greater, which is the form a hillside subdivision takes here.
For a specific Promontory lot, the practical stock question is slope and servicing on that lot, read from the City's hillside permit guidelines, not a neighbourhood average.

A hillside development permit is the rule that defines building on Promontory: under Schedule D-5 of OCP Bylaw 2025, No. 5500, a development permit is required for subdivision of land with 20% or greater slopes and for new construction or earthworks on 20% or greater slopes.

A third-party review of the application is required where the development proposal involves 30% or greater slopes, per the City's hillside permit text referring to its Development Approval Information Bylaw.

Work confined to slopes under 20% is exempt in the cases the City lists, including where the property contains only areas with natural slopes less than 20%, or where construction involves only fences or single-tier retaining walls of less than 1.2 metres in height.

The stated objectives of the hillside permit area are that new hillside development positively contributes to Chilliwack's hillside character and maintains unique hillside features such as rock outcrops, watercourses and ravines.

blocks.text: Promontory: local details a buyer would not know

items.t: The hillside permit guidelines require manufactured slopes to be re-vegetated to reflect natural conditions, and state that rock cuts are an acceptable alternative to retaining walls.
Lot grading on a hillside development must be provided on a consistent, comprehensive basis throughout the whole development, per the City's hillside guidelines.

The OCP also designates a separate Schedule D-2 Hillside Environment development permit area, listed beside the D-5 Hillside Development area, so a hillside lot can carry both an environment and a development permit layer.

The City's Sardis-Vedder parks list does not name a community park inside Promontory itself; its listed community parks for the Sardis-Vedder area are All Sappers Memorial Park, Cheam Centre Park, Sardis Park, Vedder Park and Watson Glen Park on the valley floor.
Chilliwack General Hospital at 45600 Menholm Road is the Fraser Health community hospital serving this hillside.

The cost item specific to the hill is the permit process itself: a proposal on 30% or greater slopes requires a third-party review of the application under the City's hillside rules, which is a professional cost a buyer should confirm with the City before pricing a build or addition.
Route 54 Promontory is the hillside bus, running Cottonwood Mall to Promontory via Promontory Road in the BC Transit Rider's Guide route list.
Route 56 Cultus Lake is the seasonal route in the same guide, listed for the July 1 to Labour Day period, and its routing uses the Vedder and Promontory corridor toward Cultus Lake.
Route 51 Vedder runs Vedder Road at the foot of the hill, between downtown Chilliwack and the University of the Fraser Valley Chilliwack campus.

Slope is the first due diligence item on Promontory: read the lot against Schedule D-5 Hillside Development in the OCP, confirm whether any part of the building site is at or over 20% slope, and whether the 30% third-party review trigger applies.
Check the Schedule D-2 Hillside Environment layer as well as D-5, because the OCP lists both hillside permit areas and a lot can be in either or both.
Check watercourses and ravines on the lot, which the hillside objectives name as features to be maintained, and check any creek against the Schedule D-3 Riparian Area permit area.

The hillside permit text does not give a lot-specific stability conclusion; a buyer still needs the lot's own geotechnical advice where the City requires it, rather than relying on the neighbourhood's general hillside designation.

faq.a: No, the trigger is slope, not the neighbourhood name. The City's Schedule D-5 text requires a development permit for subdivision, new construction or earthworks on 20% or greater slopes, and exempts development restricted to areas with natural slopes under 20%. A buyer should have the lot's slope read from the City's mapping and permit office before assuming a permit, a geotechnical report or neither is needed.
faq.q: Does every Promontory lot need a hillside permit?

faq.a: Route 54 Promontory is the hillside route in the BC Transit Chilliwack Rider's Guide, listed as Cottonwood Mall to Promontory via Promontory Road. The Route 54 map shows the climb from Vedder Road at Promontory Road up to the Teskey Way and Promontory Road timing point, with the Tyson and Watson area and Sardis Secondary passed on the valley-floor part of the routing.

The permit layer is different. Flat Sardis lots are governed mainly by zoning and the Sardis plan, while a Promontory lot at or over 20% slope also needs a hillside development permit, and a proposal involving 30% or greater slopes needs a third-party review of the application, per the City's Schedule D-5 text. That adds a professional report step a flat-lot buyer does not face.
